It identifies a non-monotonic relationship between retrieval recall and efficiency—both high-accuracy (exact) and low-accuracy (coarse) retrieval degrade performance—favoring high-recall approximate search instead. The system incorporates priority-aware scheduling to optimize KV-cache reuse and non-stall retrieval to eliminate retrieval-induced stalls, resulting in up to 3.4× higher throughput and 5× lower latency than state-of-the-art baselines without sacrificing generation quality.

Large Language Model (LLM)-based search agents have shown remarkable capabilities in solving complex tasks by dynamically decomposing problems and addressing them through interleaved reasoning and retrieval. However, this interleaved paradigm introduces substantial efficiency bottlenecks. First, we observe that both highly accurate and overly approximate retrieval methods degrade system efficiency: exact search incurs significant retrieval overhead, while coarse retrieval requires additional reasoning steps during generation. Second, we identify inefficiencies in system design, including improper scheduling and frequent retrieval stalls, which lead to cascading latency -- where even minor delays in retrieval amplify end-to-end inference time. To address these challenges, we introduce SearchAgent-X, a high-efficiency inference framework for LLM-based search agents. SearchAgent-X leverages high-recall approximate retrieval and incorporates two key techniques: priority-aware scheduling and non-stall retrieval. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SearchAgent-X consistently outperforms state-of-the-art systems such as vLLM and HNSW-based retrieval across diverse tasks, achieving up to 3.4$\\times$ higher throughput and 5$\\times$ lower latency, without compromising generation quality. SearchAgent-X is available at https://github.com/tiannuo-yang/SearchAgent-X.

**Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation.** Large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as agents that autonomously decide when and how to retrieve external knowledge. ReAct [1] pioneered the interleaving of reasoning traces with action steps, demonstrating that LLMs can synergistically combine chain-of-thought with tool use such as Wikipedia search. Toolformer [2] showed that LLMs can learn to decide when to call external APIs including search engines during generation. IRCoT [3] specifically interleaves retrieval with chain-of-thought reasoning for knowledge-intensive multi-step questions, showing that each reasoning step can guide the next retrieval query. Self-RAG [4] introduced special reflection tokens that allow an LLM to decide on-the-fly whether to retrieve, and to critique its own generations, trained through supervised fine-tuning. FLARE [5] proposed active retrieval during generation by detecting when the model lacks confidence and issuing forward-looking retrieval queries. More recently, Search-o1 [6] extended agentic search to large reasoning models, integrating retrieval into the extended chain-of-thought reasoning process. These works establish the paradigm of agentic RAG but primarily rely on prompting or supervised fine-tuning, without explicit optimization of the search decision process itself.

**Reinforcement Learning for Agentic Search.** A growing body of work applies reinforcement learning (RL) to train LLMs for search-augmented reasoning. Search-R1 [7] proposed an RL framework where LLMs learn to interleave reasoning with search engine calls, using outcome-based rewards and format rewards computed over structured reasoning traces. R1-Searcher [8] introduced RL-based incentives for the search capability of LLMs, using retrieval-based outcome rewards to encourage effective use of search tools. R1-Searcher++ [9] extended this approach to incentivize dynamic knowledge acquisition, explicitly rewarding the model based on whether retrieved information contributes to correct answers. RAG-R1 [10] explored multi-query parallelism, training LLMs to generate multiple search queries simultaneously to improve retrieval coverage. DecEx-RAG [11] applied process supervision to agentic RAG, optimizing both the decision to search and the execution of search queries through a process-supervised RL pipeline. Beyond Outcome Reward [12] proposed decoupling the search and answering reward signals, showing that separate reward components for search quality and answer correctness improve agent performance. Despite these advances, existing methods rely on outcome-based or coarsely-grained reward signals that do not provide explicit step-level feedback on whether each individual search decision was necessary or optimal.

**Process Rewards and Fine-Grained Supervision for LLM Reasoning.** The idea of providing process-level rather than outcome-only rewards has gained traction in LLM training. Let's Reward Step by Step [13] introduced step-level process reward models (PRMs) for mathematical reasoning, demonstrating that fine-grained supervision at each reasoning step yields better alignment than final-answer-only feedback. DeepSeek-R1 [14] showed that large-scale RL with rule-based outcome rewards can elicit sophisticated reasoning behaviors, including self-verification and reflection, without explicit process supervision. DeepSeekMath [15] introduced Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a critic-free RL algorithm that compares outputs within groups to compute relative advantages, later widely adopted for training reasoning and search agents. In the context of agentic RAG, however, process rewards remain underexplored: existing PRM methods focus on mathematical or code reasoning where step correctness is well-defined, while search trajectories present unique challenges including ambiguous step boundaries and the difficulty of determining whether a retrieval was truly necessary.

**Search Efficiency and Knowledge-Aware Retrieval.** A complementary line of work addresses the efficiency of retrieval-augmented systems by determining when retrieval is needed and when the model should rely on its parametric knowledge. When to Retrieve [16] proposed training LLMs to recognize questions that require retrieval versus those answerable from parametric knowledge alone. SeaKR [17] introduced self-aware knowledge retrieval, where the model assesses its own knowledge state to make adaptive retrieval decisions. KBM [18] delineated knowledge boundaries for LLMs to enable adaptive retrieval, training models to recognize the limits of their parametric knowledge. Several recent works specifically target suboptimal search behaviors in agentic systems. Search Wisely [19] proposed reducing over-search by modeling the model's uncertainty and suppressing searches when confidence is high. To Search or Not to Search [20] applied causal intervention to align the decision boundary of deep search agents, distinguishing necessary from unnecessary retrieval steps. AutoSearch [21] introduced adaptive search depth control via RL, learning to terminate search early when sufficient information has been gathered. Demystifying and Enhancing the Efficiency of LLM-Based Search Agents [22] conducted a systematic analysis of efficiency bottlenecks in search agents and proposed training strategies to reduce redundant retrievals. While these methods improve search efficiency through adaptive retrieval policies, confidence estimation, or coarse-grained penalties, none provides the fine-grained, step-specific feedback on individual retrieval decisions that is necessary to simultaneously suppress both over-search and under-search during training.

s2_metadata.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models

tldr.text: [research paper] ReAct introduces a prompt-based paradigm where large language models generate interleaved reasoning traces and actions, enabling dynamic, grounded reasoning through interaction with external environments. By allowing reasoning to inform action and action to refine reasoning (reason-to-act and act-to-reason), ReAct mitigates hallucination and error propagation in question answering and fact verification, while achieving significant performance gains—up to 34% and 10% absolute success rate improvements—over imitation and reinforcement learning on interactive tasks like ALFWorld and WebShop, even with one or two in-context examples. The approach enhances model interpretability by making internal reasoning and external interactions explicitly traceable to humans.

tldr.text: [research paper] Toolformer introduces a self-supervised method for large language models (LLMs) to autonomously learn tool usage via API calls without human annotations. By leveraging in-context learning to generate candidate API calls from a dataset, the model evaluates their utility through a self-supervised loss that measures improvement in next-token prediction, then fine-tunes on only the helpful calls. This enables zero-shot performance gains across downstream tasks, outperforming larger models like GPT-3 while preserving core language modeling capabilities, with no task-specific constraints or heavy supervision.

This bidirectional loop improves retrieval accuracy (up to +21 recall points) and downstream QA performance (up to +15 F1 points) across multi-step open-domain datasets, reduces factual hallucinations by up to 50%, and achieves strong gains on smaller models (e.g., Flan-T5-3B) without training, outperforming baseline one-step retrieval and existing methods in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings.

Unlike traditional RAG, which retrieves fixed, irrelevant passages indiscriminately, SELF-RAG dynamically decides retrieval necessity and uses self-generated critique tokens to select the most factually sound output, enabling controllable, verifiable, and customizable generation with improved citation accuracy and robustness across reasoning and long-form tasks.

The first stage uses a retrieve-only reward to teach retrieval invocation patterns, while the second stage employs an answer-based reward to refine the integration of retrieved knowledge for accurate responses. The method achieves superior performance on multi-hop QA benchmarks, outperforming GPT-4o-mini by up to 48.22% on HotpotQA and demonstrates strong generalization to out-of-domain and online search scenarios via a retrieval-environment-aware training design.

s2_metadata.title: R1-Searcher++: Incentivizing the Dynamic Knowledge Acquisition of LLMs via Reinforcement Learning

tldr.text: [research paper] R1-Searcher++ introduces a two-stage training framework that enables LLMs to dynamically switch between internal and external knowledge: an SFT cold-start phase ensures format compliance, followed by outcome-supervised reinforcement learning that incentivizes internal knowledge use when confident and external search when uncertain. A memory mechanism converts retrieved content into internal knowledge, enabling continuous self-improvement through memorization. Experiments on Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct show 4.3% accuracy gains over baselines and a 42.9% reduction in retrieval counts compared to vanilla RL methods, demonstrating efficient, self-sustaining knowledge acquisition.

s2_metadata.title: RAG-R1: Incentivizing the Search and Reasoning Capabilities of LLMs through Multi-query Parallelism

tldr.text: [research paper] RAG-R1 introduces a multi-query parallelism framework that transforms single-query retrieval in RAG systems into parallel, adaptive search-reasoning pipelines, enabling LLMs to dynamically leverage both internal and external knowledge during generation. By integrating format-learning SFT and outcome-based reinforcement learning, the method reduces retrieval rounds by up to 40% and inference time by 11.1% while improving accuracy on seven QA benchmarks—outperforming state-of-the-art baselines by up to 13.2%—by simultaneously exploring diverse knowledge paths in parallel rather than sequentially.

tldr.text: [research paper] DecEx-RAG introduces a process-supervised Markov Decision Process (MDP) framework for Agentic RAG, decomposing decision-making (termination and retrieval) and execution into distinct stages to enable fine-grained supervision. It proposes an efficient pruning strategy during search tree expansion that dynamically eliminates redundant branches using aggregated rollout rewards, reducing data construction time by nearly 6× while maintaining data quality. Experiments on six QA datasets show a 6.3% average performance gain over Search-R1, with superior task decomposition, dynamic retrieval, and answer generation capabilities.

tldr.text: [research paper] DeSA introduces a two-stage reinforcement learning framework that decouples search behavior optimization from final answer generation, addressing systemic deficiencies in outcome-only training such as failure to search, invalid queries, and redundant searches. By first training on retrieval recall rewards to improve search effectiveness, and then optimizing answer accuracy via outcome rewards, DeSA achieves significantly higher search recall (from 59.5% to 64.5%) and final accuracy (up to 8.0% improvement on 3B models) across seven QA benchmarks, demonstrating that search and answering are distinct objectives requiring separate optimization.

tldr.text: [research paper] The paper proposes HGS-PRM, a heuristic greedy search algorithm that leverages step-level feedback from a process-supervised reward model (PRM) during LLM inference to improve multi-step reasoning accuracy. Unlike prior methods that use PRM only in training (e.g., PPO), this work deploys PRM in decoding to guide step selection and path search, achieving superior performance on GSM8K (65.4% vs. 63.2% for CoT) and MATH (13.7% vs. 10.4%) benchmarks. The method is extended to code generation via AST-based automated PRM dataset creation, boosting HumanEval performance from 41.5% to 44.5% in Code-LLaMA-Python-13B, demonstrating broad applicability across reasoning domains.

tldr.text: [research paper] DeepSeek-R1 introduces a pure reinforcement learning (RL)-based pipeline to incentivize reasoning in LLMs without supervised fine-tuning, achieving performance comparable to OpenAI-o1-1217 via multi-stage RL and cold-start data. tldr.text: [research paper] DeepSeekMath 7B achieves 51.7% on the MATH benchmark via scalable pre-training on 120B math tokens mined from Common Crawl using a fastText-based filtering pipeline, outperforming open-source models and approaching GPT-4 performance. s2_metadata.title: When to Retrieve: Teaching LLMs to Utilize Information Retrieval Effectively

tldr.text: [research paper] Adapt-LLM is trained to autonomously decide when to retrieve external context via an information retrieval (IR) system during question answering, using a special token ⟨RET⟩ to signal the need for retrieval. The model learns to rely on its parametric memory for high-confidence, high-popularity questions and uses IR only when necessary, outperforming fixed strategies (e.g., always retrieving or always relying on memory) and matching popularity-threshold-based methods without any popularity scores. Performance gains are observed when retrieval is used, but the model's effectiveness is ultimately limited by the quality of the off-the-shelf IR system, especially in zero-shot or domain-unknown scenarios.

s2_metadata.title: SeaKR: Self-aware Knowledge Retrieval for Adaptive Retrieval Augmented Generation

tldr.text: [research paper] SeaKR introduces a self-aware adaptive RAG framework that leverages LLM internal states—specifically, consistency measures in the feed-forward network (FFN) of layers corresponding to the last generated token—to detect self-aware uncertainty. This uncertainty signals when retrieval is needed and guides both re-ranking of retrieved snippets (selecting those that reduce uncertainty most) and dynamic reasoning strategy selection (e.g., direct generation vs. comprehensive reasoning) for complex tasks. Experiments show superior performance on complex QA benchmarks, with ablation studies confirming that dynamic integration of retrieved knowledge yields greater gains than retrieval alone.

s2_metadata.title: KBM: Delineating Knowledge Boundary for Adaptive Retrieval in Large Language Models

tldr.text: [research paper] KBM introduces a novel Knowledge Boundary Model to dynamically identify when an LLM has sufficient knowledge to answer a question, thereby reducing unnecessary RAG retrievals. It proposes two soft-label generation methods—based on response accuracy and entropy (certainty)—to distinguish known vs. unknown questions without relying on golden answers, achieving up to 32.5% reduction in retrieval calls with only a 0.39% performance drop. Validated across 11 English and Chinese datasets, KBM outperforms All-RAG in dynamic knowledge, long-tail static knowledge, and multi-hop scenarios by enabling adaptive, context-aware retrieval triggering.

s2_metadata.title: Search Wisely: Mitigating Sub-optimal Agentic Searches By Reducing Uncertainty

tldr.text: [research paper] The paper identifies and quantifies over-search and under-search as pervasive inefficiencies in agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, linking these behaviors to the model's uncertainty about its knowledge boundaries. It proposes β-GRPO, a reinforcement learning method that uses confidence thresholds derived from token probabilities to reward high-certainty search decisions, resulting in a 3B model that achieves 4% higher exact match scores and significantly reduced over- and under-search rates across seven QA benchmarks.

s2_metadata.title: To Search or Not to Search: Aligning the Decision Boundary of Deep Search Agents via Causal Intervention

tldr.text: [research paper] The paper identifies a fundamental inefficiency in deep search agents—misaligned decision boundaries—that lead to either over-search (redundant queries despite sufficient knowledge) or under-search (premature termination yielding errors). It proposes a causal intervention-based diagnostic method to detect these boundary errors by comparing factual and counterfactual trajectories, and introduces Decision Boundary Alignment (DAS), which constructs preference datasets from causal feedback and optimizes agent policies via preference learning to align search decisions with optimal thresholds. Experiments show DAS effectively reduces both over- and under-search while improving accuracy and efficiency.

s2_metadata.title: AutoSearch: Adaptive Search Depth for Efficient Agentic RAG via Reinforcement Learning

tldr.text: [research paper] AutoSearch introduces a self-answer-driven reinforcement learning framework that dynamically determines the minimal sufficient search depth in agentic RAG systems by generating intermediate answers at each retrieval step. It establishes an accuracy-efficiency trade-off by rewarding attainment of the minimal depth and penalizing over-searching, with a base reward stabilizing behavior and a quality-based reward improving performance on complex queries. Experiments show superior efficiency without sacrificing accuracy across single-hop and multi-hop QA tasks.

s2_metadata.title: Demystifying and Enhancing the Efficiency of Large Language Model Based Search Agents

tldr.text: [research paper] SearchAgent-X introduces a high-efficiency inference framework for LLM-based search agents that addresses critical bottlenecks in retrieval accuracy and latency. It identifies a non-monotonic relationship between retrieval recall and efficiency—both high-accuracy (exact) and low-accuracy (coarse) retrieval degrade performance—favoring high-recall approximate search instead. The system incorporates priority-aware scheduling to optimize KV-cache reuse and non-stall retrieval to eliminate retrieval-induced stalls, resulting in up to 3.4× higher throughput and 5× lower latency than state-of-the-art baselines without sacrificing generation quality.

 abstract = "Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has emerged as a promising solution for mitigating hallucinations of large language models (LLMs) with retrieved external knowledge. \paragraph{Agentic RAG & Tool Use}
The integration of external knowledge into LLMs has evolved into more dynamic, agentic systems. Frameworks like ReAct demonstrated that LLMs can synergize reasoning and acting, paving the way for agents that can autonomously decide when and what to retrieve. This led to a new class of agentic RAG systems that interleave retrieval with multi-step reasoning, often structured as a "chain-of-thought" process . Variations like Chain-of-Retrieval and DeepRAG further refined this by structuring the retrieval process itself into sequential steps to handle complex queries. To improve the decision-making capabilities of these agents, recent work has increasingly turned to RL . RL frameworks train agents to develop optimal policies for invoking tools, including search engines. For instance, use RL and curriculum learning to enhance RAG. This aligns with a broader trend of using RL to improve general tool use in LLMs. Works like ToolRL and ToRL have shown that RL from rewards based on task success can significantly scale and improve the tool-integration capabilities of LLMs. Our work builds on this foundation, applying RL not just to achieve a correct final outcome but to optimize the efficiency of the retrieval process itself.

\paragraph{Efficient Agentic RAG & Tool Use}
While agentic RAG enhances reasoning, it often introduces inefficiency, such as redundant or unnecessary tool calls. A key research direction has been to make retrieval adaptive, triggering it only when the model's internal knowledge is insufficient. Early approaches relied on heuristics or classifiers to detect uncertainty and determine the need for retrieval . More sophisticated methods learn to assess the LLM's real-time information needs or self-awareness from its internal states to make dynamic retrieval decisions . Concurrently, RL has emerged as a powerful tool for optimizing the efficiency of tool use. In the context of RAG, RL has been used to create search-efficient models and to mitigate suboptimal search behaviors by reducing uncertainty . Works like R1-Searcher++ and other synergistic reasoning agents use RL to incentivize dynamic and necessary knowledge acquisition. ReARTeR introduces a framework with a trustworthy process reward model to score and refine each step in a RAG pipeline. This mirrors efforts in the broader tool-use domain to mitigate tool overuse. For example, SMART , SMARTCAL , and OTC train agents to be self-aware and make optimal tool calls, often using RL. and also use verifiable stepwise rewards to promote more efficient general reasoning paths. While these methods improve efficiency, they often rely on proxies like model confidence or separately trained reward models. HiPRAG differs by introducing a direct, on-the-fly evaluation of each search step's necessity, providing a more explicit training signal for efficiency.

s2_metadata.title: React-tRace: A Semantics for Understanding React Hooks
s2_metadata.abstract: React has become the most widely used web front-end framework, enabling the creation of user interfaces in a declarative and compositional manner. Hooks are a set of APIs that manage side effects in function components in React. However, their semantics are often seen as opaque to developers, leading to UI bugs. We introduce React-tRace, a formalization of the semantics of the essence of React Hooks, providing a semantics that clarifies their behavior. We demonstrate that our model captures the behavior of React, by theoretically showing that it embodies essential properties of Hooks and empirically comparing our React-tRace-definitional interpreter against a test suite. Furthermore, we showcase a practical visualization tool based on the formalization to demonstrate how developers can better understand the semantics of Hooks.

tldr.text: [research paper] REACT-TRACE introduces an operational semantics for React Hooks that formally captures their behavior across rendering phases, clarifying opaque mechanisms like state persistence and side-effect scheduling. It defines a minimal language with core constructs (useState, useEffect) and proves conformance to React’s documented invariants, enabling precise reasoning about re-renders and UI bugs. A visualizer built on this semantics allows developers to trace and inspect Hook execution, revealing how state and effects interact dynamically during rendering cycles.

 abstract = "Prompting-based large language models (LLMs) are surprisingly powerful at generating natural language reasoning steps or Chains-of-Thoughts (CoT) for multi-step question answering (QA). They struggle, however, when the necessary knowledge is either unavailable to the LLM or not up-to-date within its parameters. While using the question to retrieve relevant text from an external knowledge source helps LLMs, we observe that this one-step retrieve-and-read approach is insufficient for multi-step QA. Here, \textit{what to retrieve} depends on \textit{what has already been derived}, which in turn may depend on \textit{what was previously retrieved}. To address this, we propose IRCoT, a new approach for multi-step QA that interleaves retrieval with steps (sentences) in a CoT, guiding the retrieval with CoT and in turn using retrieved results to improve CoT. Using IRCoT with GPT3 substantially improves retrieval (up to 21 points) as well as downstream QA (up to 15 points) on four datasets: HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue, and IIRC. We observe similar substantial gains in out-of-distribution (OOD) settings as well as with much smaller models such as Flan-T5-large without additional training. IRCoT reduces model hallucination, resulting in factually more accurate CoT reasoning."

s2_metadata.title: Chain-of-Retrieval Augmented Generation
s2_metadata.abstract: This paper introduces an approach for training o1-like RAG models that retrieve and reason over relevant information step by step before generating the final answer. Conventional RAG methods usually perform a single retrieval step before the generation process, which limits their effectiveness in addressing complex queries due to imperfect retrieval results. In contrast, our proposed method, CoRAG (Chain-of-Retrieval Augmented Generation), allows the model to dynamically reformulate the query based on the evolving state. To train CoRAG effectively, we utilize rejection sampling to automatically generate intermediate retrieval chains, thereby augmenting existing RAG datasets that only provide the correct final answer. At test time, we propose various decoding strategies to scale the model's test-time compute by controlling the length and number of sampled retrieval chains. Experimental results across multiple benchmarks validate the efficacy of CoRAG, particularly in multi-hop question answering tasks, where we observe more than 10 points improvement in EM score compared to strong baselines. On the KILT benchmark, CoRAG establishes a new state-of-the-art performance across a diverse range of knowledge-intensive tasks. Furthermore, we offer comprehensive analyses to understand the scaling behavior of CoRAG, laying the groundwork for future research aimed at developing factual and grounded foundation models.

tldr.text: [research paper] CoRAG introduces a chain-of-retrieval framework where language models dynamically reformulate queries and perform iterative retrieval steps to improve factual grounding in complex multi-hop reasoning tasks. It uses rejection sampling to generate intermediate retrieval chains during training, enabling explicit training of retrieval behavior, and employs diverse test-time decoding strategies (e.g., best-of-N, tree search) to scale performance with compute. Experiments show over 10-point EM gains on multi-hop QA benchmarks and new state-of-the-art results on KILT's hidden test set, with evidence of query decomposition, flexible reformulation, and robustness across retriever quality, while revealing log-linear scaling behavior between token budget and performance.

s2_metadata.title: DeepRAG: Thinking to Retrieve Step by Step for Large Language Models
s2_metadata.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable reasoning capabilities, while their practical applications are limited by severe factual hallucinations due to limitations in the timeliness, accuracy, and comprehensiveness of their parametric knowledge. Meanwhile, enhancing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with reasoning remains challenging due to ineffective task decomposition and redundant retrieval, which can introduce noise and degrade response quality. In this paper, we propose DeepRAG, a framework that models retrieval-augmented reasoning as a Markov Decision Process (MDP), enabling reasonable and adaptive retrieval. By iteratively decomposing queries, DeepRAG dynamically determines whether to retrieve external knowledge or rely on parametric reasoning at each step. Experiments show that DeepRAG improves retrieval efficiency and boosts answer accuracy by 26.4%, demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing retrieval-augmented reasoning.

tldr.text: [research paper] DeepRAG models retrieval-augmented reasoning as a Markov Decision Process, enabling step-by-step query decomposition and adaptive retrieval decisions. It introduces a binary tree search to explore parametric vs. external knowledge paths, uses imitation learning to capture effective subquery-generation and decision patterns, and employs chain-of-calibration to refine the LLM’s awareness of its knowledge boundaries, resulting in 26.4% higher accuracy and reduced redundant retrieval by dynamically deciding when to retrieve based on evolving reasoning states.

s2_metadata.title: Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey on Agentic RAG
s2_metadata.abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized artificial intelligence (AI) by enabling human like text generation and natural language understanding. However, their reliance on static training data limits their ability to respond to dynamic, real time queries, resulting in outdated or inaccurate outputs. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a solution, enhancing LLMs by integrating real time data retrieval to provide contextually relevant and up-to-date responses. Despite its promise, traditional RAG systems are constrained by static workflows and lack the adaptability required for multistep reasoning and complex task management.\
  Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Agentic RAG) transcends these limitations by embedding autonomous AI agents into the RAG pipeline. These agents leverage agentic design patterns reflection, planning, tool use, and multiagent collaboration to dynamically manage retrieval strategies, iteratively refine contextual understanding, and adapt workflows to meet complex task requirements. This integration enables Agentic RAG systems to deliver unparalleled flexibility, scalability, and context awareness across diverse applications.\
  This survey provides a comprehensive exploration of Agentic RAG, beginning with its foundational principles and the evolution of RAG paradigms. It presents a detailed taxonomy of Agentic RAG architectures, highlights key applications in industries such as healthcare, finance, and education, and examines practical implementation strategies. Additionally, it addresses challenges in scaling these systems, ensuring ethical decision making, and optimizing performance for real-world applications, while providing detailed insights into frameworks and tools for implementing Agentic RAG.

tldr.text: Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Agentic RAG) introduces autonomous AI agents into the RAG pipeline to overcome static, linear limitations of traditional RAG systems. By integrating agentic patterns—such as reflection, planning, tool use, and multi-agent collaboration—Agentic RAG enables dynamic retrieval strategies, iterative context refinement, and adaptive workflows that support multi-step reasoning and real-time decision-making. This survey presents a comprehensive taxonomy of Agentic RAG architectures, evaluates their performance across domains like healthcare, finance, and education, and addresses implementation challenges, ethical concerns, and scalability issues.

LLMs promise to revolutionize society, yet training these foundational models poses immense challenges. Semantic vector search within large language models is a potent technique that can significantly enhance search result accuracy and relevance. Unlike traditional keyword-based search methods, semantic search utilizes the meaning and context of words to grasp the intent behind queries and deliver more precise outcomes. Elasticsearch emerges as one of the most popular tools for implementing semantic search an exceptionally scalable and robust search engine designed for indexing and searching extensive datasets. In this article, we delve into the fundamentals of semantic search and explore how to harness Elasticsearch and Transformer models to bolster large language model processing paradigms. We gain a comprehensive understanding of semantic search principles and acquire practical skills for implementing semantic search in real-world model application scenarios.

It details how Elasticsearch enables hybrid text-vector retrieval, leverages learned sparse encoders for efficient embedding storage, and supports real-time, scalable querying—particularly through direct integration with LLMs like ChatGPT. The paper analyzes existing approaches where Transformer models (e.g., BERT, T5) are fine-tuned or used in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines, emphasizing scalability, performance, and contextual accuracy in cloud environments.

s2_metadata.title: The Landscape of Agentic Reinforcement Learning for LLMs: A Survey
s2_metadata.abstract: The emergence of agentic reinforcement learning (Agentic RL) marks a paradigm shift from conventional reinforcement learning applied to large language models (LLM RL), reframing LLMs from passive sequence generators into autonomous, decision-making agents embedded in complex, dynamic worlds. This survey formalizes this conceptual shift by contrasting the degenerate single-step Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) of LLM-RL with the temporally extended, partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) that define Agentic RL. Building on this foundation, we propose a comprehensive twofold taxonomy: one organized around core agentic capabilities, including planning, tool use, memory, reasoning, self-improvement, and perception, and the other around their applications across diverse task domains. Central to our thesis is that reinforcement learning serves as the critical mechanism for transforming these capabilities from static, heuristic modules into adaptive, robust agentic behavior. To support and accelerate future research, we consolidate the landscape of open-source environments, benchmarks, and frameworks into a practical compendium. By synthesizing over five hundred recent works, this survey charts the contours of this rapidly evolving field and highlights the opportunities and challenges that will shape the development of scalable, general-purpose AI agents.

tldr.text: This survey establishes a formal taxonomy of agentic reinforcement learning (Agentic RL) by contrasting conventional LLM-RL (degenerate single-step MDPs) with agentic RL as a partially observable, temporally extended POMDP. s2_metadata.title: RAG-RL: Advancing Retrieval-Augmented Generation via RL and Curriculum Learning
s2_metadata.venue: Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
s2_metadata.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems rely on retrieval models for identifying relevant contexts and answer generation models for utilizing those contexts. However, retrievers exhibit imperfect recall and precision, limiting downstream performance. We introduce RAG-RL, an answer generation model trained not only to produce answers but also to identify and cite relevant information from larger sets of retrieved contexts, shifting some of the burden of identifying relevant documents from the retriever to the answer generator. Our approach uses curriculum learning, where the model is first trained on easier examples that include only relevant contexts. Our experiments show that these training samples enable models to acquire citation and reasoning skills with greater sample efficiency and generalizability, demonstrating strong model performance even as the number of irrelevant passages increases. We benchmark our methods on three open-domain multi-hop question answering datasets and report significant gains in answer and citation accuracy. Our experiments provide empirical insights into how easier training samples can give models stronger signals for learning specific skills (e.g., citation generation) and how different components of post-training (e.g., training set construction, rule-based rewards, training sample ordering, etc.) impact final model performance.

tldr.text: [research paper] RAG-RL introduces a reasoning language model trained via reinforcement learning and curriculum learning to directly identify and cite relevant contexts from long retrieval sets, shifting retrieval burden from retrievers to generators. The model learns citation and reasoning skills through progressively difficult training samples, achieving superior answer and citation accuracy on multi-hop QA datasets, with empirical findings showing that min-max curricula outperform linear ones and that easier samples accelerate skill acquisition, especially in distractor-rich environments.

s2_metadata.title: ToolRL: Reward is All Tool Learning Needs
s2_metadata.abstract: Current Large Language Models (LLMs) often undergo supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to acquire tool use capabilities. However, SFT struggles to generalize to unfamiliar or complex tool use scenarios. Recent advancements in reinforcement learning (RL), particularly with R1-like models, have demonstrated promising reasoning and generalization abilities. Yet, reward design for tool use presents unique challenges: multiple tools may be invoked with diverse parameters, and coarse-grained reward signals, such as answer matching, fail to offer the finegrained feedback required for effective learning. In this work, we present the first comprehensive study on reward design for tool selection and application tasks within the RL paradigm. We systematically explore a wide range of reward strategies, analyzing their types, scales, granularity, and temporal dynamics. Building on these insights, we propose a principled reward design tailored for tool use tasks and apply it to train LLMs using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Empirical evaluations across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that our approach yields robust, scalable, and stable training, achieving a 17% improvement over base models and a 15% gain over SFT models. These results highlight the critical role of thoughtful reward design in enhancing the tool use capabilities and generalization performance of LLMs. All the codes are released to facilitate future research.

tldr.text: [research paper] The paper presents the first systematic study of reward design for Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) in LLMs via reinforcement learning, identifying key dimensions—type, scale, granularity, and dynamics—of reward signals. It demonstrates that fine-grained, dynamically scaled rewards outperform coarse or static ones, leading to 17% gains over base models and 15% over SFT models, with improved generalization, proactiveness, and metacognition in tool selection and application across diverse tasks. The findings establish a principled, algorithm-agnostic framework for effective RL-based agentic tool use.

s2_metadata.abstract: Despite their impressive performance on diverse tasks, large language models (LMs) still struggle with tasks requiring rich world knowledge, implying the limitations of relying solely on their parameters to encode a wealth of world knowledge. This paper aims to understand LMs' strengths and limitations in memorizing factual knowledge, by conducting large-scale knowledge probing experiments of 10 models and 4 augmentation methods on PopQA, our new open-domain QA dataset with 14k questions. We find that LMs struggle with less popular factual knowledge, and that scaling fails to appreciably improve memorization of factual knowledge in the long tail. tldr.text: [research paper] Large language models (LLMs) poorly memorize factual knowledge about long-tail entities, even as model scale increases—performance remains low for less popular entities, with GPT-3 and larger models achieving only ~16–19% accuracy on the least popular questions. s2_metadata.title: To Retrieve or Not to Retrieve? Uncertainty Detection for Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation
s2_metadata.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation equips large language models with the capability to retrieve external knowledge, thereby mitigating hallucinations by incorporating information beyond the model's intrinsic abilities. However, most prior works have focused on invoking retrieval deterministically, which makes it unsuitable for tasks such as long-form question answering. Instead, dynamically performing retrieval by invoking it only when the underlying LLM lacks the required knowledge can be more efficient. In this context, we delve deeper into the question, "To Retrieve or Not to Retrieve?" by exploring multiple uncertainty detection methods. We evaluate these methods for the task of long-form question answering, employing dynamic retrieval, and present our comparisons. Our findings suggest that uncertainty detection metrics, such as Degree Matrix Jaccard and Eccentricity, can reduce the number of retrieval calls by almost half, with only a slight reduction in question-answering accuracy.

tldr.text: [research paper] The paper evaluates uncertainty detection methods—such as Semantic Sets, Degree Matrix Jaccard, and Eccentricity—to dynamically trigger retrieval in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) for long-form multi-hop question answering. By assessing response diversity via pairwise similarity and clustering, these metrics reduce unnecessary retrieval calls by nearly 50% while maintaining minimal accuracy loss, demonstrating that uncertainty-based conditional retrieval improves RAG efficiency without sacrificing reliability.

s2_metadata.title: SUGAR: Leveraging Contextual Confidence for Smarter Retrieval
s2_metadata.venue: IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing
s2_metadata.abstract: Bearing in mind the limited parametric knowledge of Large Language Models (LLMs), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) which supplies them with the relevant external knowledge has served as an approach to mitigate the issue of hallucinations to a certain extent. However, uniformly retrieving supporting context makes response generation source-inefficient, as triggering the retriever is not always necessary, or even inaccurate, when a model gets distracted by noisy retrieved content and produces an unhelpful answer. Motivated by these issues, we introduce Semantic Uncertainty Guided Adaptive Retrieval (SUGAR), where we leverage context-based entropy to actively decide whether to retrieve and to further determine between single-step and multi-step retrieval. Our empirical results show that selective retrieval guided by semantic uncertainty estimation improves the performance across diverse question answering tasks, as well as achieves a more efficient inference.

tldr.text: [research paper] SUGAR introduces Semantic Uncertainty Guided Adaptive Retrieval (SUGAR), a novel retrieval strategy that uses semantic entropy—instead of token-level predictive entropy—to assess whether an LLM is confident in answering a question using only its internal knowledge. By accounting for linguistic invariance (i.e., different surface forms expressing the same meaning), semantic entropy avoids overconfidence in semantically redundant outputs and enables precise, context-aware decisions: no retrieval for confident cases, single-step retrieval for moderate uncertainty, and multi-step retrieval for high uncertainty. Empirical results on SQuAD, Natural Questions, and TriviaQA show that SUGAR improves factual accuracy and reduces hallucinations while significantly reducing unnecessary retrieval overhead, achieving better performance than baseline methods without requiring training or task-specific tuning.

s2_metadata.abstract: Increasing test-time compute for LLMs shows promise across domains but remains underexplored in code generation, despite extensive study in math. s2_metadata.title: C*: Unifying Programming and Verification in C
s2_metadata.abstract:
Ensuring the correct functionality of systems software, given its safety-critical and low-level nature, is a primary focus in formal verification research and applications. Despite advances in verification tooling, conventional programmers are rarely involved in the verification of their own code, resulting in higher development and maintenance costs for verified software. A key barrier to programmer participation in verification practices is the disconnect of environments and paradigms between programming and verification practices, which limits accessibility and real-time verification.\

It enables real-time verification by allowing programmers to embed proof-code blocks alongside implementation code, facilitating interactive updates to the current proof state. Its expressive and extensible proof support allows users to build reusable libraries of logical definitions, theorems, and programmable proof automation. Crucially, C* unifies implementation and proof code development by using C as the common language.\
  We implemented a prototype of C* and evaluated it on a representative benchmark of small C programs and a challenging real-world case study: the attach function of pKVM's buddy allocator. Our results demonstrate that C* supports the verification of a broad subset of C programming idioms and effectively handles complex reasoning tasks in real-world scenarios.

s2_metadata.title: SEM: Reinforcement Learning for Search-Efficient Large Language Models
s2_metadata.abstract: Recent advancements in Large Language Models(LLMs) have demonstrated their capabilities not only in reasoning but also in invoking external tools, particularly search engines. However, teaching models to discern when to invoke search and when to rely on their internal knowledge remains a significant challenge. Existing reinforcement learning approaches often lead to redundant search behaviors, resulting in inefficiencies and over-cost. In this paper, we propose SEM, a novel post-training reinforcement learning framework that explicitly trains LLMs to optimize search usage. By constructing a balanced dataset combining MuSiQue and MMLU, we create scenarios where the model must learn to distinguish between questions it can answer directly and those requiring external retrieval. We design a structured reasoning template and employ Group Relative Policy Optimization(GRPO) to post-train the model's search behaviors. Our reward function encourages accurate answering without unnecessary search while promoting effective retrieval when needed. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly reduces redundant search operations while maintaining or improving answer accuracy across multiple challenging benchmarks. This framework advances the model's reasoning efficiency and extends its capability to judiciously leverage external knowledge.

tldr.text: [research paper] SEM introduces a post-training reinforcement learning framework that trains large language models to distinguish between questions answerable from internal knowledge and those requiring external search. By constructing a balanced dataset from Musique and MMLU, and using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a structured reward function that penalizes redundant searches and rewards strategic tool invocation, the model learns to suppress unnecessary search while maintaining high accuracy. Experiments show significant reduction in redundant search operations without compromising answer quality, improving reasoning efficiency and search-awareness in uncertain scenarios.

s2_metadata.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are powerful but prone to hallucinations due to static knowledge. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) helps by injecting external information, but current methods often are costly, generalize poorly, or ignore the internal knowledge of the model. In this paper, we introduce R1-Searcher++, a novel framework designed to train LLMs to adaptively leverage both internal and external knowledge sources. R1-Searcher++ employs a two-stage training strategy: an initial SFT Cold-start phase for preliminary format learning, followed by RL for Dynamic Knowledge Acquisition. The RL stage uses outcome-supervision to encourage exploration, incorporates a reward mechanism for internal knowledge utilization, and integrates a memorization mechanism to continuously assimilate retrieved information, thereby enriching the model's internal knowledge. By leveraging internal knowledge and external search engine, the model continuously improves its capabilities, enabling efficient retrieval-augmented reasoning. Our experiments demonstrate that R1-Searcher++ outperforms previous RAG and reasoning methods and achieves efficient retrieval. The code is available at https://github.com/RUCAIBox/R1-Searcher-plus.

tldr.text: [research paper] R1-Searcher++ introduces a two-stage training framework that enables LLMs to dynamically switch between internal and external knowledge: an SFT cold-start phase ensures format compliance, followed by outcome-supervised reinforcement learning that incentivizes internal knowledge use when confident and external search when uncertain. A memory mechanism converts retrieved content into internal knowledge, enabling continuous self-improvement through memorization. Experiments on Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct show 4.3% accuracy gains over baselines and a 42.9% reduction in retrieval counts compared to vanilla RL methods, demonstrating efficient, self-sustaining knowledge acquisition.

s2_metadata.title: Reinforced Internal-External Knowledge Synergistic Reasoning for Efficient Adaptive Search Agent
s2_metadata.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a common strategy to reduce hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs). While reinforcement learning (RL) can enable LLMs to act as search agents by activating retrieval capabilities, existing ones often underutilize their internal knowledge. This can lead to redundant retrievals, potential harmful knowledge conflicts, and increased inference latency. To address these limitations, an efficient and adaptive search agent capable of discerning optimal retrieval timing and synergistically integrating parametric (internal) and retrieved (external) knowledge is in urgent need. This paper introduces the Reinforced Internal-External Knowledge Synergistic Reasoning Agent (IKEA), which could indentify its own knowledge boundary and prioritize the utilization of internal knowledge, resorting to external search only when internal knowledge is deemed insufficient. This is achieved using a novel knowledge-boundary aware reward function and a knowledge-boundary aware training dataset. These are designed for internal-external knowledge synergy oriented RL, incentivizing the model to deliver accurate answers, minimize unnecessary retrievals, and encourage appropriate external searches when its own knowledge is lacking. Evaluations across multiple knowledge reasoning tasks demonstrate that IKEA significantly outperforms baseline methods, reduces retrieval frequency significantly, and exhibits robust generalization capabilities.

tldr.text: [research paper] IKEA introduces a reinforcement learning-based adaptive search agent that dynamically determines retrieval timing by modeling self-knowledge boundaries, enabling prioritization of internal (parametric) knowledge over external search. A knowledge-boundary aware reward function and balanced training dataset jointly incentivize accurate reasoning, minimal unnecessary retrievals, and appropriate external queries when internal knowledge is insufficient, significantly reducing retrieval frequency while improving performance on both single-hop and multi-hop knowledge reasoning tasks.

s2_metadata.title: ReARTeR: Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning with Trustworthy Process Rewarding
s2_metadata.venue: Annual International ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval
s2_metadata.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems for Large Language Models (LLMs) hold promise in knowledge-intensive tasks but face limitations in complex multi-step reasoning. While recent methods have integrated RAG with chain-of-thought reasoning or test-time search using Process Reward Models (PRMs), these approaches encounter challenges such as a lack of explanations, bias in PRM training data, early-step bias in PRM scores, and insufficient post-training optimization of reasoning potential. To address these issues, we propose Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning through Trustworthy Process Rewarding (ReARTeR), a framework that enhances RAG systems' reasoning capabilities through post-training and test-time scaling. At test time, ReARTeR introduces Trustworthy Process Rewarding via a Process Reward Model for accurate scalar scoring and a Process Explanation Model (PEM) for generating natural language explanations, enabling step refinement. During post-training, it utilizes Monte Carlo Tree Search guided by Trustworthy Process Rewarding to collect high-quality step-level preference data, optimized through Iterative Preference Optimization. ReARTeR addresses three core challenges: (1) misalignment between PRM and PEM, tackled through off-policy preference learning; (2) bias in PRM training data, mitigated by balanced annotation methods and stronger annotations for challenging examples; and (3) early-step bias in PRM, resolved through a temporal-difference-based look-ahead search strategy. Experimental results on multi-step reasoning benchmarks demonstrate significant improvements, underscoring ReARTeR's potential to advance the reasoning capabilities of RAG systems.

tldr.text: [research paper] ReARTeR introduces a dual-phase framework—test-time Trustworthy Process Rewarding and post-training via Monte Carlo Tree Search guided by process rewards—to enhance reasoning in retrieval-augmented generation. It addresses key limitations in existing methods by aligning Process Reward Models (PRMs) and Process Explanation Models (PEMs) through off-policy preference learning, mitigating PRM data bias via balanced annotations from strong models/humans, and reducing early-step bias using a temporal-difference-based look-ahead search. The framework enables step-level refinement with interpretable explanations and achieves superior multi-step reasoning performance on benchmark datasets through both inference-time scaling and offline reinforcement optimization.

s2_metadata.title: SMART: Self-Aware Agent for Tool Overuse Mitigation
s2_metadata.venue: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
s2_metadata.abstract: Current Large Language Model (LLM) agents demonstrate strong reasoning and tool use capabilities, but often lack self-awareness, failing to balance these approaches effectively. This imbalance leads to Tool Overuse, where models unnecessarily rely on external tools for tasks solvable with parametric knowledge, increasing computational overhead. Inspired by human metacognition, we introduce SMART (Strategic Model-Aware Reasoning with Tools), a paradigm that enhances an agent's self-awareness to optimize task handling and reduce tool overuse. To support this paradigm, we introduce SMART-ER, a dataset spanning three domains, where reasoning alternates between parametric knowledge and tool-dependent steps, with each step enriched by rationales explaining when tools are necessary. Through supervised training, we develop SMARTAgent, a family of models that dynamically balance parametric knowledge and tool use. Evaluations show that SMARTAgent reduces tool use by 24% while improving performance by over 37%, enabling 7B-scale models to match its 70B counterpart and GPT-4o. Additionally, SMARTAgent generalizes to out-of-distribution test data like GSM8K and MINTQA, maintaining accuracy with just one-fifth the tool calls. These highlight the potential of strategic tool use to enhance reasoning, mitigate overuse, and bridge the gap between model size and performance, advancing intelligent and resource-efficient agent designs.

tldr.text: [research paper] SMART introduces a metacognition-inspired framework to mitigate tool overuse in LLM agents by enabling self-aware decision-making between parametric knowledge and external tool use. SMART-ER, a multi-domain dataset with rationale-labeled reasoning steps, trains SMARTAgent to dynamically balance reasoning paths, reducing tool calls by 24% and improving performance by 37% while enabling small-scale models to match large-scale counterparts and maintaining accuracy under out-of-distribution conditions with only 20% of the tool calls.

s2_metadata.venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
s2_metadata.abstract: The tool-use ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) has a profound impact on a wide range of industrial applications. However, LLMs' self-control and calibration capability in appropriately using tools remains understudied. The problem is consequential as it raises potential risks of degraded performance and poses a threat to the trustworthiness of the models. In this paper, we conduct a study on a family of state-of-the-art LLMs on three datasets with two mainstream tool-use frameworks. Our study reveals the tool-abuse behavior of LLMs, a tendency for models to misuse tools with overconfidence. We also find that this is a common issue regardless of model capability. Accordingly, we propose a novel approach, \\textit{SMARTCAL}, to mitigate the observed issues, and our results show an average of 8.6 percent increase in the QA performance and a 21.6 percent decrease in Expected Calibration Error (ECE) compared to baseline models.

s2_metadata.title: Scaling Relationship on Learning Mathematical Reasoning with Large Language Models
s2_metadata.abstract: Mathematical reasoning is a challenging task for large language models (LLMs), while the scaling relationship of it with respect to LLM capacity is under-explored. In this paper, we investigate how the pre-training loss, supervised data amount, and augmented data amount influence the reasoning performances of a supervised LLM. We find that pre-training loss is a better indicator of the model's performance than the model's parameter count. We apply supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with different amounts of supervised data and empirically find a log-linear relation between data amount and model performance, and we find better models improve less with enlarged supervised datasets. To augment more data samples for improving model performances without any human effort, we propose to apply Rejection sampling Fine-Tuning (RFT). RFT uses supervised models to generate and collect correct reasoning paths as augmented fine-tuning datasets. We find with augmented samples containing more distinct reasoning paths, RFT improves mathematical reasoning performance more for LLMs. We also find RFT brings more improvement for less performant LLMs. Furthermore, we combine rejection samples from multiple models which push LLaMA-7B to an accuracy of 49.3\\% on GSM8K which outperforms the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) accuracy of 35.9\\% significantly.

tldr.text: [empirical research paper] This paper establishes a data-driven scaling analysis of mathematical reasoning in supervised large language models (LLMs), revealing that pre-training loss is a stronger performance predictor than model size. It demonstrates a log-linear relationship between supervised data volume and model accuracy, with diminishing returns for high-performing models. The key innovation is Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RFT), which uses LLMs to generate correct reasoning paths via rejection sampling, yielding significant gains—up to +13.4% on GSM8K for LLaMA-7B—especially when combining samples across multiple models, thereby improving reasoning generalization through diverse path exposure.

s2_metadata.title: Promoting Efficient Reasoning with Verifiable Stepwise Reward
s2_metadata.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have recently achieved significant progress in complex reasoning tasks, aided by reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. However, LRMs often suffer from overthinking, expending excessive computation on simple problems and reducing efficiency. Existing efficient reasoning methods typically require accurate task assessment to preset token budgets or select reasoning modes, which limits their flexibility and reliability. In this work, we revisit the essence of overthinking and identify that encouraging effective steps while penalizing ineffective ones is key to its solution. To this end, we propose a novel rule-based verifiable stepwise reward mechanism (VSRM), which assigns rewards based on the performance of intermediate states in the reasoning trajectory. This approach is intuitive and naturally fits the step-by-step nature of reasoning tasks. We conduct extensive experiments on standard mathematical reasoning benchmarks, including AIME24 and AIME25, by integrating VSRM with PPO and Reinforce++. Results show that our method achieves substantial output length reduction while maintaining original reasoning performance, striking an optimal balance between efficiency and accuracy. Further analysis of overthinking frequency and pass@k score before and after training demonstrates that our approach in deed effectively suppresses ineffective steps and encourages effective reasoning, fundamentally alleviating the overthinking problem. All code will be released upon acceptance.

tldr.text: [research paper] The paper identifies overthinking in large reasoning models (LRMs) as a result of excessive computation on ineffective intermediate steps during step-by-step reasoning. It proposes a rule-based verifiable stepwise reward mechanism (VSRM) that assigns rewards to individual reasoning steps based on correctness variations across truncated sub-trajectories, eliminating the need for unstable process-level reward models. Experiments on AIME24/AIME25 benchmarks show significant output length reduction (up to 40%) with maintained or improved accuracy, effectively suppressing redundant steps by directly rewarding beneficial reasoning transitions and penalizing non-contributive ones.

s2_metadata.title: Beyond Correctness: Harmonizing Process and Outcome Rewards through RL Training
s2_metadata.abstract:
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has emerged to be a predominant paradigm for mathematical reasoning tasks, offering stable improvements in reasoning ability. However, Outcome Reward Models (ORMs) in RLVR are too coarse-grained to distinguish flawed reasoning within correct answers or valid reasoning within incorrect answers. This lack of granularity introduces noisy and misleading gradients significantly and hinders further progress in reasoning process quality. While Process Reward Models (PRMs) offer fine-grained guidance for intermediate steps, they frequently suffer from inaccuracies and are susceptible to reward hacking.\
  To resolve this dilemma, we introduce PRocess cOnsistency Filter (PROF), an effective data process curation method that harmonizes noisy, fine-grained process rewards with accurate, coarse-grained outcome rewards. Rather than naively blending PRM and ORM in the objective function (arXiv:archive/2506.18896), PROF leverages their complementary strengths through consistency-driven sample selection. Our approach retains correct responses with higher averaged process values and incorrect responses with lower averaged process values, while maintaining positive/negative training sample balance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method not only consistently improves the final accuracy over $4\\%$ compared to the blending approaches, but also strengthens the quality of intermediate reasoning steps. Codes and training recipes are available at https://github.com/Chenluye99/PROF.

tldr.text: [research paper] PROF introduces a data curation framework that filters training samples based on consistency between fine-grained process rewards (PRMs) and coarse-grained outcome rewards (ORMs), eliminating conflicting trajectories—such as correct answers with flawed reasoning or incorrect answers with valid steps—without directly incorporating PRMs into the training gradient. By separately ranking correct and incorrect responses according to process-outcome alignment and maintaining balanced training ratios, PROF avoids reward hacking and entropy collapse, achieving +4% accuracy gains and improving intermediate reasoning quality on math benchmarks without requiring additional PRM fine-tuning.

claims.text: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as agents that autonomously decide when and how to retrieve external knowledge.
ReAct pioneered the interleaving of reasoning traces with action steps, demonstrating that LLMs can synergistically combine chain-of-thought with tool use such as Wikipedia search.
Toolformer showed that LLMs can learn to decide when to call external APIs including search engines during generation.
IRCoT specifically interleaves retrieval with chain-of-thought reasoning for knowledge-intensive multi-step questions, showing that each reasoning step can guide the next retrieval query.
Self-RAG introduced special reflection tokens that allow an LLM to decide on-the-fly whether to retrieve, and to critique its own generations, trained through supervised fine-tuning.
FLARE proposed active retrieval during generation by detecting when the model lacks confidence and issuing forward-looking retrieval queries.
Search-o1 extended agentic search to large reasoning models, integrating retrieval into the extended chain-of-thought reasoning process.
These works establish the paradigm of agentic RAG but primarily rely on prompting or supervised fine-tuning, without explicit optimization of the search decision process itself.
A growing body of work applies reinforcement learning (RL) to train LLMs for search-augmented reasoning.
Search-R1 proposed an RL framework where LLMs learn to interleave reasoning with search engine calls, using outcome-based rewards and format rewards computed over structured reasoning traces.
R1-Searcher introduced RL-based incentives for the search capability of LLMs, using retrieval-based outcome rewards to encourage effective use of search tools.
R1-Searcher++ incentivizes dynamic knowledge acquisition by explicitly rewarding the model based on whether retrieved information contributes to correct answers.
RAG-R1 explored multi-query parallelism, training LLMs to generate multiple search queries simultaneously to improve retrieval coverage.
DecEx-RAG applied process supervision to agentic RAG, optimizing both the decision to search and the execution of search queries through a process-supervised RL pipeline.
Beyond Outcome Reward proposed decoupling the search and answering reward signals, showing that separate reward components for search quality and answer correctness improve agent performance.

Despite these advances, existing methods rely on outcome-based or coarsely-grained reward signals that do not provide explicit step-level feedback on whether each individual search decision was necessary or optimal.
The idea of providing process-level rather than outcome-only rewards has gained traction in LLM training.

Let's Reward Step by Step introduced step-level process reward models (PRMs) for mathematical reasoning, demonstrating that fine-grained supervision at each reasoning step yields better alignment than final-answer-only feedback.
DeepSeek-R1 showed that large-scale RL with rule-based outcome rewards can elicit sophisticated reasoning behaviors, including self-verification and reflection, without explicit process supervision.

DeepSeekMath introduced Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a critic-free RL algorithm that compares outputs within groups to compute relative advantages, later widely adopted for training reasoning and search agents.

In the context of agentic RAG, process rewards remain underexplored: existing PRM methods focus on mathematical or code reasoning where step correctness is well-defined, while search trajectories present unique challenges including ambiguous step boundaries and the difficulty of determining whether a retrieval was truly necessary.
A complementary line of work addresses the efficiency of retrieval-augmented systems by determining when retrieval is needed and when the model should rely on its parametric knowledge.
When to Retrieve proposed training LLMs to recognize questions that require retrieval versus those answerable from parametric knowledge alone.
SeaKR introduced self-aware knowledge retrieval, where the model assesses its own knowledge state to make adaptive retrieval decisions.
KBM delineated knowledge boundaries for LLMs to enable adaptive retrieval, training models to recognize the limits of their parametric knowledge.
Several recent works specifically target suboptimal search behaviors in agentic systems.
Search Wisely proposed reducing over-search by modeling the model's uncertainty and suppressing searches when confidence is high.
To Search or Not to Search applied causal intervention to align the decision boundary of deep search agents, distinguishing necessary from unnecessary retrieval steps.
AutoSearch introduced adaptive search depth control via RL, learning to terminate search early when sufficient information has been gathered.

Demystifying and Enhancing the Efficiency of LLM-Based Search Agents conducted a systematic analysis of efficiency bottlenecks in search agents and proposed training strategies to reduce redundant retrievals.

While these methods improve search efficiency through adaptive retrieval policies, confidence estimation, or coarse-grained penalties, none provides the fine-grained, step-specific feedback on individual retrieval decisions that is necessary to simultaneously suppress both over-search and under-search during training.

retrieved_evidence.text: [research paper] SearchAgent-X introduces a high-efficiency inference framework for LLM-based search agents that addresses critical bottlenecks in retrieval accuracy and latency. It identifies a non-monotonic relationship between retrieval recall and efficiency—both high-accuracy (exact) and low-accuracy (coarse) retrieval degrade performance—favoring high-recall approximate search instead. The system incorporates priority-aware scheduling to optimize KV-cache reuse and non-stall retrieval to eliminate retrieval-induced stalls, resulting in up to 3.4× higher throughput and 5× lower latency than state-of-the-art baselines without sacrificing generation quality.

Large Language Model (LLM)-based search agents have shown remarkable capabilities in solving complex tasks by dynamically decomposing problems and addressing them through interleaved reasoning and retrieval. However, this interleaved paradigm introduces substantial efficiency bottlenecks. First, we observe that both highly accurate and overly approximate retrieval methods degrade system efficiency: exact search incurs significant retrieval overhead, while coarse retrieval requires additional reasoning steps during generation. Second, we identify inefficiencies in system design, including improper scheduling and frequent retrieval stalls, which lead to cascading latency -- where even minor delays in retrieval amplify end-to-end inference time. To address these challenges, we introduce SearchAgent-X, a high-efficiency inference framework for LLM-based search agents. SearchAgent-X leverages high-recall approximate retrieval and incorporates two key techniques: priority-aware scheduling and non-stall retrieval. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SearchAgent-X consistently outperforms state-of-the-art systems such as vLLM and HNSW-based retrieval across diverse tasks, achieving up to 3.4$\\times$ higher throughput and 5$\\times$ lower latency, without compromising generation quality. SearchAgent-X is available at https://github.com/tiannuo-yang/SearchAgent-X.

Large Language Model (LLM)-based search agents have shown remarkable capabilities in solving complex tasks by dynamically decomposing problems and addressing them through interleaved reasoning and retrieval. However, this interleaved paradigm introduces substantial efficiency bottlenecks. First, we observe that both highly accurate and overly approximate retrieval methods degrade system efficiency: exact search incurs significant retrieval overhead, while coarse retrieval requires additional reasoning steps during generation. Second, we identify inefficiencies in system design, including improper scheduling and frequent retrieval stalls, which lead to cascading latency -- where even minor delays in retrieval amplify end-to-end inference time. To address these challenges, we introduce SearchAgent-X, a high-efficiency inference framework for LLM-based search agents. SearchAgent-X leverages high-recall approximate retrieval and incorporates two key techniques: priority-aware scheduling and non-stall retrieval. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SearchAgent-X consistently outperforms state-of-the-art systems such as vLLM and HNSW-based retrieval across diverse tasks, achieving up to 3.4$\\times$ higher throughput and 5$\\times$ lower latency, without compromising generation quality. SearchAgent-X is available at https://github.com/tiannuo-yang/SearchAgent-X.
